title: Short Stuff: Balloonfest
summary: Short Stuff episode on Balloonfest '86, a 1986 publicity stunt by the United Way of Cleveland to improve the city's image and set a world record by releasing millions of helium balloons over downtown Cleveland. Covers the idea from George Fraser, balloon artist Treb Hinding (who built the balloon arch for Share and Greg Allmond's son's third birthday), the 250 by 150 foot netted structure on Public Square, the planned two million balloons versus the roughly 1.5 million actually released on a windy, cold September Saturday, the balloons drifting over Lake Erie, the Cuyahoga River, traffic, the Burke Lakefront Airport shutdown, a horse farm injury lawsuit, and the Coast Guard calling off a search for two missing fishermen. The stunt cost about $500,000 and earned a Guinness record, but became an environmental mess.

segments.title: Introduction and Cleveland's image problem
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce Balloonfest '86, a United Way of Cleveland publicity stunt meant to rehabilitate the city's reputation as the 'mistake on the Lake' after the Cuyahoga River fire. They note the idea came from George Fraser.

segments.title: Planning and the balloon artist
segments.summary: The United Way hired balloon artist Treb Hinding, known for Olympic opening ceremonies, Super Bowls, and inventing the balloon arch, which first appeared at Share and Greg Allmond's son Elijah Blue's third birthday. Planning took about six months.

segments.title: The netted structure and the record goal
segments.summary: A 250 by 150 foot, three-story netted structure was built on Public Square, with netting made by the company that supplied Space Shuttle cargo nets. Volunteers filled balloons inside it. The goal was two million balloons, to beat Disneyland's record of 1.2 million balloons from 1990.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break before the discussion of the weather and the release.

segments.title: Weather and the release
segments.summary: Cold, windy late-September weather by Lake Erie led organizers to stop at about 1.5 million balloons instead of two million. The net was lifted on Saturday around 1:50 and the balloons were released, rising as a writhing mass near the Terminal Tower.

segments.title: Balloons come back down: damage and rescue
segments.summary: Cold air pushed many balloons back down. They landed on Lake Erie, the Cuyahoga River, traffic, and a horse farm where a woman (Louise Nowakowski) raised Arabian horses; the horses were injured and she sued. Burke Lakefront Airport shut for half an hour and there were highway collisions. The Coast Guard suspended its search for two missing fishermen, Raymond Broderick and Bernard Solzer, because balloons looked like life jackets. Costs reached about $500,000, and there were settlements.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts reflect that the stunt replaced one environmental reputation with another, joke about lessons learned, and sign off.
